item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #23] Safety Wrapper & 1st Semester Final Presentation
item.content:encoded:
As we entered June, the Maeumjigi team completed the major developments of the 1st semester Capstone project and focused entirely on building safety nets and preparing for the final presentation.

The Victory of the 2:1 Ratio and the Safety Wrapper​

"What was our chosen model?" "We decided on 2:1. Now design a method to use a safety_wrapper as a safety lock for our Main Large Language Model (LLM) (2:1)."

As a result of the 4th fine-tuning, we selected the model mixed with a 2:1 ratio of 'emotional' to 'daily' chat as our final LLM. However, given the nature of a suicide prevention chatbot, we could not allow even a single hallucination or fatal wrong answer.

To prevent this, we introduced a Safety Wrapper. It verifies the input and output of the LLM, and if a high-risk situation (Active Suicidality) is detected, the architecture instantly switches to a pre-defined crisis response protocol.

Cloud Server (EC2) Budget and Final Presentation​

"We need an AWS EC2 quote. What's the budget for 5 months of g5.2xlarge?" "Draft the 1st_semester_final_presentation.pptx based on our progress!"

We calculated the Amazon EC2 GPU server budget to run the verified chatbot for 5 months during the summer vacation.

And on June 18th, we gathered all the achievements of our backend, frontend, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to complete the 1st Semester Final Presentation (PPTX)!

The long and arduous 1st semester of the Maeumjigi Capstone development has successfully concluded. We will deploy the system to the server over the summer and return with a more advanced service in the 2nd semester!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #22] 4th Fine-Tuning Complete! Architecture Design & Final Report
item.content:encoded:
In the final week of May (27th-30th), we dedicated our efforts to wrapping up the results of the highly anticipated 4th Fine-Tuning (fine_tuning_4) and solidifying the system's framework.

Final Checkpoint 4400 and Graph Analysis​

"Qwen35-9B_mixed_7_3/checkpoints/checkpoint-4400/adapter_config.json"

The 4th fine-tuning model, trained with a mix of daily casual chat and emotional counseling data, finally finished training and yielded the optimal weight: checkpoint-4400.

In previous fine-tunings, there was an overfitting issue where the model would respond in an overly serious counseling mode even to casual chat. As a result of experimenting with the data mix ratio, the model has finally been reborn as a 'perceptive' chatbot that perfectly distinguishes between and appropriately responds to daily conversation and serious crisis counseling!

We visualized all evaluation metrics with matplotlib graphs to prove the performance differences at a glance.

Chatbot System Architecture Design and Final Report​

"chatbot_architecture.html generation complete" "Please write the results of fine_tuning_4 as a report (.docx)."

To serve the verified model as a real app, we designed the entire system architecture and Knowledge Graph integration plan under the name chatbot_architecture.html.

And on May 30th, with the Artificial Intelligence (AI)'s help, we automatically generated the fine_tuning_4_report.docx, successfully concluding Phase 1 of our fine-tuning project. The report bluntly contains the actual response text comparisons between the original base model and our fine-tuned model, proving that all our hard work was not in vain!

With this, the breathless May dev logs of the Maeumjigi project are all wrapped up. What new challenges await in June?

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #21] Optimizing Data Mix Ratios and Starting the 4th Fine-Tuning
item.content:encoded:
On May 21st and 22nd, the Maeumjigi Capstone team embarked on massive data generation and preparation for the 4th Fine-Tuning (fine_tuning_4).

The Tug-of-War Between Emotional and Daily Conversations​

While testing the 3rd fine-tuning model, I discovered a critical issue.

"When fine-tuning with the haiku_pred dataset, the responses seem too heavily skewed towards emotional counseling. How should we fine-tune to maintain the original model's daily conversation abilities?"

Our goal is a 'suicide prevention counselor conveying warm empathy', but the model was showing signs of overfitting, giving overly serious and emotional responses even to mundane questions like "How's the weather?" or "What should I eat?".

To solve this, we planned an experiment to train the model by mixing emotional data and daily chat data at appropriate ratios.

Generating 10,000 v6 Emotion Dataset Entries via Application Programming Interface (API)​

"Unify to 512 tokens / Average 500 tokens per entry / 20 Personas / File: v6.jsonl"

To create the best dataset, I used the Anthropic API (Haiku) Batch mode to generate a staggering 10,000 entries of emotional conversation data (Emotion_train_dataset_v6.jsonl). Though there was a frustrating moment when the API batch ran in the background without showing progress, I filled in the missing entries with an additional script (fill_v6.py) to complete the 10,000 count.

Finding the Golden Ratio (fine_tuning_4)​

"Emotion_train_dataset_v6.jsonl is complete. Now make a 7:3 ratio dataset, a 2:1 ratio, and a 5:5 ratio dataset." "This 4th fine-tuning will be based on the training dataset mix ratio (mixed_2_1, mixed_5_5, mixed_7_3) instead of alpha values."

The 4th fine-tuning has now become an arena to verify which data ratio perfectly harmonizes the Artificial Intelligence (AI)'s 'daily casualness' with 'professional counseling'. We generated three versions of the dataset and started injecting them into the Qwen3.5-9B model!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Sim-to-Real: Hardware Transfer via Arduino Uno, HC-06 Bluetooth & ArUco Vision Tracking (#5)
item.description: Deploying the simulation-trained 648-bin Q-Learning policy onto a physical 2-wheeled Arduino Uno robot using ceiling webcam homography and real-time ArUco 6-DoF marker pose tracking.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Severe computational constraints on microcontrollers (Arduino Uno ATmega328P with only 2KB SRAM), non-linear wheel slip, noisy ultrasonic sensing, and the classical Reality Gap between Webots simulation physics and physical hardware.
  • Solution: Designed a distributed I/O architecture (HC-06 Bluetooth at 115,200 baud) where a host PC runs OpenCV vision processing and Q-Table inference while the Arduino handles low-level PWM motor actuation. Overhead camera lens distortion correction and ArUco marker homography (vision.py) deliver sub-centimeter real-time (x, y, θ) tracking.
  • Result: Zero-shot transfer of the simulation-trained 648-state Q-Table achieved an 86.7% target reaching success rate (26/30 trials) in a physical 1.2m × 1.2m arena, successfully closing the reality gap without real-world fine-tuning.

1. The Challenge of Sim-to-Real: Navigating the Reality Gap​

In virtual Webots simulations, surface friction coefficients remain idealized, wheel motors rotate with deterministic precision, and simulated distance sensors yield noiseless measurements. Real hardware, however, introduces unpredictable physical perturbations:

  1. Severe Memory & Compute Bottlenecks: The Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) operates with only 32KB flash memory and 2KB SRAM. Running deep neural networks or heavy matrix operations directly on-chip is physically impossible.
  2. Sensor Noise & Blind Angles: Inexpensive ultrasonic rangefinders suffer from specular reflection at shallow incidence angles, reporting 0 or spiking to maximum range when pinging smooth acrylic boundaries.
  3. Wheel Slip & Odometry Drift: Minor variations in wheel friction and motor gearboxes cause differential-drive robots to veer off-course even when commanded to drive straight, making dead-reckoning odometry completely unreliable.

2. Distributed Control Architecture: Host PC (Brain) ↔ Arduino (Muscle)​

To overcome microcontroller limitations, we decoupled high-level reasoning from low-level actuation: "PC as the brain, Arduino as the muscle."

flowchart TD
    subgraph CeilingCam["Ceiling Vision System (Overhead Camera)"]
        Cam["FHD Webcam (30 FPS)"]
        Aruco["ArUco Marker Detection (DICT_4X4_50)<br>Perspective Homography (homography.npy)"]
        Cam --> Aruco
    end

    subgraph PC["Host PC (Python Engine)"]
        Pose["Robot Pose Estimation (x, y, θ)"]
        Disc["648-bin Discretizer"]
        QL["Trained Q-Table (ε=0)"]
        BT_Host["HC-06 Bluetooth SPP (115200 baud)"]
        
        Aruco --> Pose --> Disc --> QL --> BT_Host
    end

    subgraph Robot["Physical Mobile Robot (Real Hardware)"]
        BT_Slave["HC-06 Bluetooth Receiver"]
        MCU["Arduino Uno (Firmware)"]
        Motors["L298N Dual H-Bridge + Geared DC Motors"]
        
        BT_Host <-->|"Action Byte [0..3]<br>Ack/Status"| BT_Slave --> MCU --> Motors
    end
  • Host PC Pipeline: An overhead webcam captures the complete arena top-down, tracking an ArUco fiducial marker mounted on top of the robot at 30 FPS. The robot's planar pose (x, y, θ) is calculated and mapped into the discrete 648-state space to retrieve the optimal greedy action from the Q-Table.
  • HC-06 Serial Communication: To minimize Round-Trip Time (RTT) over the Bluetooth Serial Port Profile (SPP), the transmission baud rate was upgraded from the default 9,600 to 115,200 bps, sustaining a low-latency 30~50Hz control loop.
  • Arduino Firmware (arduino_firmware.ino): Upon receiving single-byte action commands (0: Forward, 1: Backward, 2: Turn Left, 3: Turn Right), the microcontroller modulates PWM pins on the L298N motor driver for precise tick-based open-loop pulses.

3. Overhead Camera Homography & ArUco Vision Tracking​

To measure robot positioning and obstacle proximity with millimeter accuracy across the real arena, we built an OpenCV-based top-down computer vision pipeline.

📐 Perspective Rectification & Homography (calib_auto.py)​

  1. Checkerboard Distortion Calibration: To eliminate barrel distortion from wide-angle webcam lenses, intrinsic camera matrix (K) and distortion coefficients (D) were pre-computed using a standard 9×6 checkerboard.
  2. Perspective Homography: To project the angled camera viewpoint into a canonical 1.2m × 1.2m square bird's-eye view, a 3×3 perspective homography matrix (homography.npy) was established from the 4 marked arena corner coordinates.

💻 ArUco Marker Pose Tracking Implementation (vision.py)​

import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load ArUco dictionary and detection parameters
aruco_dict = cv2.aruco.getPredefinedDictionary(cv2.aruco.DICT_4X4_50)
parameters = cv2.aruco.DetectorParameters()
detector = cv2.aruco.ArucoDetector(aruco_dict, parameters)

def get_robot_pose(frame, homography_matrix):
    """Calculates planar coordinates (x, y) and heading angle (theta) from rectified image."""
    warped = cv2.warpPerspective(frame, homography_matrix, (600, 600))
    corners, ids, _ = detector.detectMarkers(warped)
    
    if ids is not None and len(ids) > 0:
        c = corners[0][0]
        center_x = float(np.mean(c[:, 0]))
        center_y = float(np.mean(c[:, 1]))
        
        # Calculate heading angle (theta) from marker front edge vector
        front_x = (c[0][0] + c[1][0]) / 2.0
        front_y = (c[0][1] + c[1][1]) / 2.0
        theta = np.arctan2(front_y - center_y, front_x - center_x)
        
        return center_x, center_y, theta
    return None

4. Hardware Troubleshooting & Real-World Deployment Results​

Transitioning from simulation to physical operation revealed critical edge cases addressed through robust engineering countermeasures:

Symptom (Troubleshooting)Root CauseEngineering Solution
Robot drifts sideways during forward commandGearbox friction differences between left & right DC motorsImplemented an interactive calibration script (ble_vision_turn_calib.py) to apply dynamic PWM trim offsets
Runaway behavior during Bluetooth disconnectPacket drops under RF interference causing robot to retain last commandEmbedded a 200ms communication watchdog timer in firmware to immediately cut motor power upon signal loss
Intermittent ArUco marker detection lossSpecular glare from ceiling fluorescent lighting on glossy marker surfaceFine-tuned adaptive thresholding parameters and added a 1D Kalman Filter position extrapolator

🏆 Final Real-World Benchmark​

  • Autonomous Goal Reaching Rate: Tested across 30 independent trials in the physical 1.2m × 1.2m obstacle arena, the robot achieved an 86.7% success rate (26/30 successful arrivals).
  • Leveraging just 2,592 pre-computed discrete Q-values (~2.5 KB), the agent navigated complex physical obstacles without any real-world gradient updates.

5. Concluding the RL Q-Learning Dev Log Series​

With this final Sim-to-Real deployment, our 5-part RL Q-Learning Robotics series reaches its conclusion:

  1. #1: 648-Bin State Discretization & Webots TCP Socket IPC Architecture
  2. #2: Tabular Q-Learning $\epsilon$-Decay Exploration & Multi-Objective Reward Shaping
  3. #3: Overcoming Arena Local Minima in 12-Wall Environments via Headless Pipelines
  4. #4: Quantitative Benchmark with evaluate_qlearning vs. SARSA & DQN
  5. #5: Sim-to-Real Hardware Transfer via Arduino Uno, Bluetooth SPP & ArUco Vision

From foundational simulator modeling and algorithmic tuning to multi-seed automation and physical hardware deployment, this series documented the complete lifecycle of reinforcement learning for embedded robotics. Stay tuned for future deep dives into our next projects!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Deterministic Evaluation via evaluate_qlearning & Benchmark vs. DQN and SARSA (#4)
item.description: Zero-exploration (ε=0) deterministic evaluation pipeline with evaluate_qlearning.py, examining path efficiency, near-miss metrics, and benchmark comparisons against DQN and SARSA.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Objective: Measure the pure, deterministic performance of the learned greedy policy (ε=0) without exploration noise, validating real-world deployability.
  • Methodology: Implemented evaluate_qlearning.py running 30 independent trials across 5 round-robin evaluation seeds, rigorously tracking success rates, path efficiency vs. theoretical shortest routes, and obstacle near-miss counts.
  • Result: Tabular Q-Learning attained a 93.3% deterministic success rate in the 12-wall arena with superior path smoothness and ultra-low 0.02ms inference latency, outperforming heavier DQN and SARSA baselines.

1. Quantitative Evaluation Pipeline (evaluate_qlearning.py)​

Training reward curves are inherently noisy due to $\epsilon$-greedy exploration. To evaluate the true deployment capability of our agent, we must test the purely deterministic policy ($\epsilon = 0$).

We built an evaluation runner that loads the saved Q-table (qlearning_qtable.npy) and evaluates the agent across 5 distinct test seeds (EVAL_SEEDS = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)).

flowchart LR
    Model["Trained Q-Table<br>(qlearning_qtable.npy)"] --> Agent["Greedy Agent<br>(ε = 0 Fixed)"]
    EvalSeeds["5 Test Seeds<br>(EVAL_SEEDS 0..4)"] --> Webots["Webots Simulator<br>(30 Evaluation Trials)"]
    Agent <--> Webots
    Webots --> CSV["Trace & Metric Logging<br>(eval_log.csv / traces)"]

💻 Evaluation Loop Architecture​

# evaluate_qlearning.py excerpt
agent = QLearningAgent(seed=0)
agent.load(model_path) # Load trained Q-Table

for ep in range(n_episodes):
    env_seed = EVAL_SEEDS[ep % len(EVAL_SEEDS)]
    raw, info = env.reset(seed=env_seed, return_info=True)
    s = discretize(raw)
    
    for t in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        a = agent.act(s, deterministic=True) # Pure argmax Q(s, a)
        raw_next, r, done, info = env.step(a)
        s = discretize(raw_next)
        
        # Log trajectory coordinates and near-misses (dist <= 0.15m)
        record_metrics(info)
        if done: break

2. Comprehensive Evaluation Metrics​

  1. Success Rate: Percentage of runs reaching the target radius (0.10m) within 150 steps without collision.
  2. Path Efficiency: Ratio of theoretical shortest path distance (L_shortest) to actual traversed path length (L_actual). Path Efficiency (%) = (Shortest Path / Actual Path) × 100%
  3. Near-Miss Frequency: Number of steps where obstacle distance dipped below 0.15m.
  4. Oscillation Count: Metric penalizing back-and-forth steering jitter.

3. Algorithm Benchmark: Tabular Q-Learning vs. SARSA vs. DQN​

Comparative evaluation in the identical Webots 12-wall arena across the three reinforcement learning algorithms revealed clear performance trade-offs:

MetricTabular Q-Learning (Ours)SARSA (On-policy)Deep Q-Network (DQN)
Learning ParadigmOff-policy TD(0)On-policy TD(0)Neural Network (Deep RL)
Parameter Size2,592 floats (~2.5 KB)2,592 floats (~2.5 KB)~150,000 weights (~600 KB)
Deterministic Success Rate (obstacle12)93.3%86.7%90.0%
Average Steps per Episode41.2 steps48.5 steps44.7 steps
Per-Step Inference Latency0.02 ms (NumPy array lookup)0.02 ms2.15 ms (PyTorch forward pass)
Near-Miss FrequencyLow (balanced detour)Minimal (excessively conservative)Moderate

🔍 In-Depth Behavioral Analysis​

  • Why Q-Learning Excels: By evaluating max_a' Q(s', a'), off-policy Q-Learning ignores transient exploratory collisions during training, settling on the shortest feasible detour path.
  • SARSA's Conservative Bias: On-policy updates factor in exploration penalties, causing SARSA to over-correct and choose excessively long, inefficient detours to avoid walls at all costs.
  • DQN's Trade-off: DQN handles continuous inputs well, but training stability requires replay buffers and target networks, while its 2.15ms latency and GPU requirement impose severe constraints on lightweight microcontrollers like Arduino.

4. Evaluation Takeaways​

Our discrete 648-bin Tabular Q-Learning model requires just 2.5 KB of memory, yet matched and exceeded deep neural network models in success rate (93.3%) and real-time execution speed.

5. What's Next?​

With simulation benchmarks thoroughly concluded, the ultimate milestone remains: transferring policy to reality (Sim-to-Real).

In our final Episode #5, we will detail the hardware integration: deploying our policy to a 2-wheel differential Arduino Uno robot, communicating via HC-06 Bluetooth, and tracking ground-truth position via ceiling webcam checkerboard calibration and ArUco markers!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Conquering Local Minima in 12-Wall Obstacles: Multi-Seed Headless Simulation (#3)
item.description: Overcoming the Local Minima dilemma in complex 12-wall obstacle environments (obstacle12) and orchestrating high-speed automated multi-seed Webots simulations.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: When a goal lies directly behind an obstacle, the myopic nature of distance-delta rewards (+0.1 × Δdist) pulls the robot into head-on collisions, trapping it in severe Local Minima.
  • Solution: Integrated 3-way head-scan obstacle perception (front/left/right) with long-horizon Bellman value propagation (γ=0.99), alongside an automated PowerShell Webots Headless pipeline (headless_run.ps1) executing multi-seed training across seeds 0, 1, and 2.
  • Result: The agent successfully learned robust detour policies in the 12-wall arena, achieving a 90%+ goal success rate after 600 episodes.

1. The Obstacle Challenge: The Local Minima Trap​

In an empty arena (no_obstacle), navigating is simply a matter of steering toward the target heading. However, introducing 12 interior walls (obstacle12) unveiled a critical bottleneck in reward design:

flowchart TD
    Start["Start (Robot)"]
    Wall["Obstacle Wall"]
    Goal["Target Goal"]
    
    Start -->|"Direct drive (greedy distance reward)"| Wall
    Wall -.->|"Collision & deadlocked (Local Minima)"| Wall
    Start ==>|"Detour Policy<br>Accepts temporary distance penalty"| Goal
  • The Dilemma: When the target is directly on the other side of an interior wall, driving straight ahead leads directly to collision.
  • Reward Conflict: Circumnavigating the wall requires moving temporarily away from the goal (negative distance delta). Under naive exploration, the agent enters a deadlock—spinning or timing out against the wall.

2. Solution Strategy: Head-Scan Perception & Value Backpropagation​

Overcoming this trap relies on coupling 3-directional head-scan perception with a high discount factor ($\gamma = 0.99$):

  1. Perceptual State Discretization:
    • Attempting to advance while front_distance = Danger yields a heavy collision penalty (-1.0).
    • Sweeping the sensor head left and right reveals free avenues (left_distance = Safe or right_distance = Safe), encouraging lateral turns.
  2. Long-Term Temporal Difference Credit Assignment:
    • Although turning away temporarily depresses the step reward, successfully rounding the wall and reaching the target yields the substantial terminal reward (+1.0).
    • Backpropagated through $Q(s, a)$ with $\gamma = 0.99$, the agent gradually learns that detour steps possess higher expected return than head-on approaches.

3. Webots Headless Automation Pipeline​

Rigorous reinforcement learning requires multi-seed validation (Seeds 0, 1, 2). Running 1,500 episodes interactively in the Webots GUI three times would take many hours.

We automated this with a headless_run.ps1 PowerShell script, launching Webots in high-speed, no-render mode (--mode=fast --no-rendering):

💻 Automated Pipeline (headless_run.ps1)​

# Launch Webots in background headless fast mode
$webotsProc = Start-Process -FilePath $WebotsExe `
    -ArgumentList @("--mode=fast", "--no-rendering", "--stdout", "--stderr", $WorldFile) `
    -PassThru

# Train agent over socket IPC
python train_qlearning.py --scenario obstacle12 --seed 0 --episodes 1500

# Cleanup process and generate performance plots
Stop-Process -Id $webotsProc.Id -Force
python -m qlearning.plot_curves --log-dir logs/obstacle12/seed_0

4. Empirical Evaluation: Cross-Environment Learning Curves​

The graph above contrasts convergence across 3 random seeds between the unobstructed world (no_obstacle) and the 12-wall obstacle world (obstacle12).

📊 Benchmark Metrics​

MetricEmpty Arena (no_obstacle)12-Wall Arena (obstacle12)
Initial Convergence~300 - 400 episodes~600 - 800 episodes
Final Success Rate (100-ep MA)98.5% - 99.2%91.4% - 94.8%
Mean Steps per Episode15 - 22 steps38 - 52 steps (detour path)
Cross-Seed VarianceNegligible (highly stable)Moderate (exploration path dependency)
  • Extended Exploration: In obstacle12, discovering viable detour corridors requires approximately 200 additional episodes of random trials, keeping the average reward depressed until episode 400.
  • Detour Mastery: Beyond episode 800, all seeds stabilize above 90% success, confirming that the agent reliably maneuvers through tight gaps without collisions.

5. What's Next?​

Our 648-bin Tabular Q-Learning model successfully navigates maze-like obstacle configurations.

In Episode #4, we will load the saved model checkpoints (models/*.npy) to benchmark greedy, deterministic performance using evaluate_qlearning.py and analyze comparative metrics against DQN and SARSA!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Tabular Q-Learning Implementation & Reward Shaping Tuning (#2)
item.description: In-depth breakdown of Tabular Q-Learning TD(0) update formulas, exponential epsilon-decay exploration, and dense reward shaping to overcome sparse rewards in mobile robot navigation.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Sparse reward setups (+1.0 at goal, -1.0 at collision) cause severe exploration delays, causing the agent to wander or spin for thousands of episodes before stumbling upon the target.
  • Solution: Implemented a multi-objective Dense Reward Shaping mechanism combining potential-based Euclidean distance delta rewards (+0.1 × Δdist) with step (-0.01), turning (-0.01), and backward (-0.05) penalties, paired with exponential epsilon decay (1.0 → 0.05).
  • Result: The moving average reward shifted into a steady positive regime (0.7+) within 500 episodes in the no_obstacle scenario, achieving a 98%+ goal success rate.

1. Tabular Q-Learning Update Formula & Agent Architecture​

Tabular Q-Learning is an off-policy Temporal Difference (TD(0)) algorithm grounded in the Bellman Optimality Equation.

The agent maintains an action-value table $Q(s, a)$ structured as a 2D NumPy array of shape $(648, 4)$. Using the experience transition tuple $(s, a, r, s', done)$ streamed from the Webots socket server, the $Q$-values are updated in real time via:

📐 Q-Learning TD(0) Update Rule​

Target = r + γ * max_a' Q(s', a') * (1 - done)
TD Error = Target - Q(s, a)
Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + α * TD Error
  • Learning Rate ($\alpha = 0.1$): Balances the rate of incorporating new feedback versus retaining historical estimates.
  • Discount Factor ($\gamma = 0.99$): Values long-term future returns, critical for multi-step navigation.
  • Terminal Masking (1 - done): Clamps future expectations to zero upon goal arrival or collision, isolating the terminal reward.

💻 Agent Core Implementation (qlearning_agent.py)​

import numpy as np

class QLearningAgent:
    def __init__(self, n_states=648, n_actions=4, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99,
                 eps_start=1.0, eps_min=0.05, eps_decay=0.995, seed=0):
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions), dtype=np.float64)
        self.alpha = float(alpha)
        self.gamma = float(gamma)
        self.epsilon = float(eps_start)
        self.eps_min = float(eps_min)
        self.eps_decay = float(eps_decay)
        self.n_actions = int(n_actions)

    def act(self, s: int, deterministic: bool = False) -> int:
        """ε-Greedy behavior policy: Exploration vs. Exploitation"""
        if (not deterministic) and self.rng.random() < self.epsilon:
            return int(self.rng.integers(self.n_actions))
        return int(np.argmax(self.Q[s]))

    def update(self, s: int, a: int, r: float, s_next: int, done: bool) -> float:
        """TD(0) Off-policy Q-Table update"""
        target = r if done else r + self.gamma * float(np.max(self.Q[s_next]))
        td_error = target - self.Q[s, a]
        self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * td_error
        return float(td_error)

    def decay_epsilon(self):
        """Exponential decay executed at the end of each episode"""
        self.epsilon = max(self.eps_min, self.epsilon * self.eps_decay)

2. Exponential Epsilon-Greedy Decay Strategy​

At the start of training, the agent has zero domain knowledge, requiring $\epsilon = 1.0$ (100% random exploration) to discover the arena boundaries.

However, an uncurbed exploration rate induces perpetual collisions even after the optimal path has been resolved. We apply per-episode exponential decay:

ε_(ep+1) = max(ε_min, ε_ep × 0.995)

  • Episode 1: $\epsilon = 1.0$ (Full exploration)
  • Episode 300: $\epsilon \approx 0.22$ (Shift toward exploiting high Q-values)
  • Episode 600: $\epsilon = 0.05$ (Floor exploration rate $\epsilon__min$, 95% greedy execution)

3. Dense Reward Shaping for Sparse Navigation​

A fundamental challenge in mobile robotics is sparse reward feedback. In a $1.2m \times 1.2m$ arena, moving randomly yields zero reward until the robot coincidentally intersects the $0.10m$ goal tolerance.

To guide convergence, we engineered a Dense Reward Shaping schedule inside the Webots controller (RL_controller.py):

Reward ComponentValueDesign Objective & Physical Effect
Goal Reached (REWARD_GOAL)+1.0Terminal reward on successful target arrival
Wall/Obstacle Collision (REWARD_COLLISION)-1.0Severe penalty on physical impact
Distance Delta Reward (REWARD_DELTA_SCALE)+0.1 × ΔdistImmediate feedback proportional to Euclidean distance reduction
Step Time Penalty (REWARD_STEP)-0.01Prevents idling and incentivizes shortest paths
Turning Penalty (REWARD_TURN)-0.01Suppresses unproductive spinning behavior
Backward Penalty (REWARD_BACKWARD)-0.05Discourages inefficient reverse driving

🔍 Mathematical Principle of Distance Delta​

Δdist = dist_prev - dist_curr

  • Driving $0.05m$ toward the target awards $+0.1 \times 0.05 = +0.005$ immediately.
  • Conversely, driving away incurs an instant penalty, allowing the agent to align its heading with the target within the first 100 episodes.

4. Empirical Evaluation: Reward and Success Curves​

Training for 1,500 episodes in the no_obstacle world demonstrated remarkable convergence matching our theoretical expectations.

📈 Convergence Milestones​

  1. Episodes 0 ~ 200 (Exploration Phase):
    • Frequent wall collisions and 150-step timeouts keep the moving average reward in the negative range (-0.4 ~ -0.2).
  2. Episodes 200 ~ 500 (Ascent Phase):
    • As distance-delta rewards propagate through the Q-Table, the policy establishes a strong forward-driving preference whenever goal_heading is centered.
    • Success rate surges from 20% to over 80%.
  3. Episodes 500 ~ 1,500 (Asymptotic Convergence):
    • With $\epsilon$ settled at 0.05, average steps per episode plummet from 150 (timeout) to 15 ~ 22 steps.
    • The 100-episode moving average success rate converges above 98.5%.

5. What's Next?​

We have proven that Tabular Q-Learning over 648 states solves empty arena navigation cleanly.

However, real-world environments are packed with walls and obstacles. In Episode #3, we will investigate the obstacle12 and obstacle_hard maps, examining how our agent handles local minima traps and running multi-seed parallel training!

item.title: [Webots Robotics] Q-Learning Autonomous Navigation: 648-Bin State Discretization & Socket Architecture (#1)
item.description: Designing a 648-bin state space discretizer and a TCP socket IPC architecture for Webots mobile robot autonomous navigation with tabular Q-Learning.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Continuous sensor readings (distance & heading) cause a state-space explosion for tabular Q-learning, and synchronous IPC with the Webots simulator requires low-latency coordination.
  • Solution: Designed a geometrically partitioned 5-dimensional continuous sensor mapper producing 3 × 8 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 648 discrete states (discretizer.py) and a line-delimited JSON IPC socket pipeline over TCP port 5000.
  • Result: Achieved $O(1)$ fast Q-Table indexing and reliable 32ms physics synchronization between the simulator and Python agent.

1. Project Background: Why Webots and Q-Learning?​

Enabling an autonomous differential-drive robot to navigate an unknown indoor arena and reach a target while avoiding obstacles is a foundational robotics challenge. While Deep Reinforcement Learning (DQN, PPO) handles complex inputs, it demands high computational overhead and lacks straightforward interpretability.

In this project, we apply classical Tabular Q-Learning (Off-policy TD(0)) to a mobile robot in the Webots 3D physics engine. Our objective is to establish an optimal, mathematically verifiable navigation and obstacle avoidance policy in a 1.2m × 1.2m indoor arena.

2. System Architecture: Webots Controller ↔ Python RL Engine​

The system is decoupled into two clean tiers: the Webots simulation server and the Python RL client.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Webots["Webots 3D Simulator (localhost:5000)"]
        Robot["Supervisor Robot<br>(Ultrasonic Sensor + Wheels)"]
        HeadScan["Head-scan Mechanism<br>(Left/Right 1.1 rad servo)"]
        Server["TCP Socket Server<br>(Line-delimited JSON)"]
        Robot -→ HeadScan -→ Server
    end

    subgraph Python["Python RL Engine (Client)"]
        Env["WebotsEnv (gym-like)<br>reset() / step()"]
        Disc["Discretizer<br>(Continuous → 0~647 Bin)"]
        Agent["QLearningAgent<br>(Q-Table 648x4)"]
        Env -→ Disc -→ Agent
    end

    Server <-→|"request: {type: step, action: 0..3}<br>response: {state: [...], reward, done}"| Env
  • Webots Controller (RL_controller.py): Executes action commands for 480ms (15 simulation ticks $×$ 32ms) and rotates a head-mounted ultrasonic sensor left and right by 1.1 rad ($\approx 63°$) to eliminate blind spots.
  • Socket Protocol: Lightweight line-delimited JSON over TCP localhost:5000:
    • Request: {"type": "step", "action": 0} (0: Forward, 1: Backward, 2: Turn Left, 3: Turn Right)
    • Response: {"state": [0.45, 0.12, 0.35, 0.28, 0.40], "reward": 0.05, "done": false, "info": {...}}

3. Discretizing Continuous Sensors into 648 States​

To apply tabular Q-learning, continuous floats must be mapped into finite discrete states. We selected 5 crucial observation variables based on kinematic relevance:

FeatureBinsThresholdsSemantic Meaning
goal_distance3[0.6m, 1.2m]Near, Mid, Far
goal_heading8$[-π, π]$ (8 sectors, $45°$ each)Front, Front-Right, Right, Back-Right, Back, Back-Left, Left, Front-Left
front_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger/Collision, Caution, Safe
left_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger, Caution, Safe
right_distance3[0.15m, 0.30m]Danger, Caution, Safe

Total State Count: N_states = 3 × 8 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 648

The resulting Q-Table requires only $648 × 4 = 2,592$ floating-point entries, allowing sub-millisecond memory updates and zero GPU overhead.

💻 State Discretization Code (discretizer.py)​

import numpy as np

# Dimension boundaries
N_GOAL_D, N_GOAL_H, N_FRONT, N_LEFT, N_RIGHT = 3, 8, 3, 3, 3
N_STATES = N_GOAL_D * N_GOAL_H * N_FRONT * N_LEFT * N_RIGHT  # 648

_HEADING_BINS = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 9)[1:-1]
_NEAR_BINS    = np.array([0.15, 0.30])
_DIST_BINS    = np.array([0.6, 1.2])

def discretize(state_dict: dict) → int:
    """Maps 5-tuple continuous sensor readings to an integer in [0, 647]."""
    gd = int(np.digitize(state_dict["goal_distance"], _DIST_BINS))
    gh = int(np.digitize(state_dict["goal_heading"], _HEADING_BINS))
    df = int(np.digitize(state_dict["front_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))
    dl = int(np.digitize(state_dict["left_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))
    dr = int(np.digitize(state_dict["right_distance"], _NEAR_BINS))

    # Compute flattened 1D index
    index = ((((gd * N_GOAL_H + gh) * N_FRONT + df) * N_LEFT + dl) * N_RIGHT + dr)
    return int(index)

4. Head-Scan Mechanism & Collision Logic​

A fixed forward-facing sensor leaves lateral blind spots. We implemented an active Head-Scan routine:

  1. Step Execution: Drive motors at 3.0 rad/s for 480ms.
  2. Head Rotation: Sweep head servo +1.1 rad to read left distance, then -1.1 rad for right distance.
  3. Re-center: Return head to 0 rad and refresh front distance.
  4. Terminal Conditions:
    • Goal Reached: Euclidean distance $<= 0.10m \rightarrow$ success (done = True, reward $+1.0$)
    • Collision: Any distance $<= 0.08m \rightarrow$ failure (done = True, reward $-1.0$)

5. What's Next?​

With the simulator environment, TCP socket IPC, and 648-bin state discretization established, our agent is ready for reinforcement learning.

In Episode #2, we will cover the mathematical implementation of Tabular Q-Learning, $\epsilon$-greedy exploration decay, and reward function tuning!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #18] Expanding Inference Tokens and Comparing 2nd Fine-Tuning Results
item.content:encoded:
On May 13th, after fixing the hardcoding bugs discovered yesterday, we finally resumed proper inference testing for the 2nd round fine-tuned models.

The Cause of Short Answers: Increase the Token Length!​

While meticulously reviewing the inference results, I felt that the answers from the Llama33-70B_a8 model were still strangely short and rigid.

"This is one of Llama33-70B_a8's answers. I feel that max_seq_length and max_new_tokens are too small. I want to increase them. Looking at the VRAM status, how much can I increase them?"

After calculating the available VRAM space (39.8GB at the time) with the Artificial Intelligence (AI), we boldly increased max_new_tokens (the maximum number of words generated) to 384. The result was a massive success!

[Before] "It must be really hard to feel that way. It is important to talk to a professional."
[After] "It must be really hard to feel that way. However, having these thoughts is not a sign that you are weak, but a signal that you are carrying too much burden right now. I highly recommend slowly unraveling these emotions with a professional."

By simply increasing the token allowance, the model maintained its context to the end and began pouring out much deeper and warmer sentences of empathy. The model had been holding its tongue because it was trapped in a limited token count.

Alpha Value Comparison Analysis (a=8 vs a=16)​

The results for the biggest objective of the 2nd fine-tuning—the performance difference based on the LoRA hyperparameter alpha—were also out. By analyzing the logs piled up in the fine_tuning_2 folder, we generated graphs like 05_alpha_comparison_daily.png. With rank=16 fixed, we clearly visualized how the model's overfitting patterns and final answer quality differed when given alpha=8 versus alpha=16.

Ultimately, models granted the correct hyperparameters and ample token length were finally getting closer to the true 'Maeumjigi' (Heart-keeper) we had originally planned. It seems our mid-term presentation preparations will wrap up very smoothly!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #17] 2nd Fine-Tuning Complete & The Trap of the Automation Pipeline
item.content:encoded:
The 2nd round of fine-tuning (fine_tuning_2) parallel training, which was ambitiously started to correct the LoRA hyperparameter mistake (alpha/rank setup error), finally ended on May 12th!

Extracting the Best Checkpoint and Building the Inference Pipeline​

The fine-tuning for 3 models with 6 hyperparameter combinations was all completed. I immediately compared the eval_loss to extract the best performing checkpoints and moved them to the adapter folders for each model.

I also created a new run_test_20_30.sh script to run evaluation and result comparison all at once in the background on the server.

"Currently, the HCX-Text-1p5B models generated 12 outputs in 15 minutes. GPU Util is 1.6GB per graphics card..."

However, the inference speed was still hopeless. Even the lightest 1.5B model couldn't even generate 1 answer per minute. The VRAM usage was only 1.6GB, meaning a bottleneck occurred because the Batch Size was set to 1. On top of this, server storage issues forced us to urgently migrate the project's base path from ~/home/ to ~/home/data/temporary/, causing a huge fuss to modify all script paths.

Falling into the Trap of Hardcoding​

After painstakingly running all the evaluation codes, I discovered a horrifying fact.

"Why is MODEL_ALIAS hardcoded to 'Qwen35-9B_a16' in 20_eval_ft_models.ipynb?" "So in the server logs, even for 20_eval_HCX-Text-1p5B_a8.ipynb, MODEL_ALIAS was defined as 'Qwen35-9B_a16'. You're telling me it's normal that the filename and model name are different?"

Yes. While writing the evaluation automation script, I accidentally hardcoded MODEL_ALIAS. The script diligently copied files to test the HCX model, but inside the code, it kept repeatedly loading only the Qwen35-9B_a16 model and doing the same inference over and over!

It was a day that made me realize once again that fine-tuning is not a science, but a battle of meticulousness. I'll have to fix this hardcoded bug and run the inferences again tomorrow.

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #16] Fatal Mistake, 2nd Fine-Tuning, and React Native App Launch
item.content:encoded:
May 8th was the day we were building our capstone design mid-term presentation (PPT) based on the fine-tuning results. However, while happily filling in the slides, I discovered a massive, chilling mistake.

Discovering the Fatal LoRA Hyperparameter Mistake​

I was refining the model structure diagrams and hyperparameter info with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) for the PPT.

"Looking at the fine-tuning examples, the answers are shorter than the base model. I think this is because setting LoRA's r to 8 and alpha to 16 reduced the intermediate features too much..." "Wait, it was a/r? I thought it was r/a...??? I really applied LoRA greedily..."

When fine-tuning with LoRA, it's standard to set the alpha value equal to or twice the rank value. However, I completely misunderstood the scaling ratio equation, setting it in a way that either severely suppressed or excessively amplified the weight updates. No wonder the fine-tuned models' answers were unnaturally short and chopped off—the fault lay right at my fingertips.

The Decision for 2nd Round Fine-Tuning (fine_tuning_2)​

Although we already had the 1st round results, we couldn't just move on for a perfect 'Maeumjigi'. I immediately created a fine_tuning_2 folder and decided on a 2nd round of fine-tuning.

"The models to use this time are HCX-Text-1p5B, Llama33-70B, and Qwen35-9B. Train on MIG-0 with rank=16, alpha=16, and on MIG-1 with rank=16, a=8." "Extract the top 2000 longest entries from Daily_train_dataset.jsonl and create a file named Daily_train_dataset_long.jsonl."

To prevent the answers from becoming too short, we extracted only the top 2000 datasets with the longest text length. We also split our MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) resources to run parallel training, directly comparing the performance differences based on the rank and alpha ratios.

Starting Frontend (App) Development While the Backend Trains​

While the models fell back into the cycle of training, I didn't just sit around. I finally started developing the frontend app where actual users will meet 'Maeumjigi'!

"I need to show a QR code to run maeum-app... but when I type npx go start, I only get an error message. How and where can the QR code be shown?"

I created the maeum-app project using React Native (Expo) and struggled to launch the local server and connect it to my smartphone. I even mistakenly typed npx go start instead of expo, but I finally succeeded in pulling up the Expo QR code and setting up the app icons (assets/logo.png). It was a thrilling day where the brain of the backend (AI) and the face of the frontend (App) were being built simultaneously.

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #15] Visualizing Fine-Tuning Results of 5 Models & Local Environment Setup

Visualization and Local Setup for Model Comparison​

"Can't 30_comparison.ipynb run on my laptop too?" "Please tell me how to install pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, and bert_score on the currently selected kernel."

"What is the difference between the faint line and the thick line? Bring the training loss and eval loss for each model and visualize them as graphs." "Remove the thick line and make the faint line clearer and save it."

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #14] All Fine-Tuning Completed and Parallel Inference (Eval) Pipeline Built
item.content:encoded:
On May 6th, we finally escaped the long swamp of fine-tuning! After several nights of work and hyperparameter tuning, the training for mid-size models like HCX-Omni-8B and Qwen35-9B was successfully completed.

Fine-Tuning Complete, Analyzing the Logs​

As the training progressed, we could see the loss values decreasing stably.

step= 1200  loss=0.9698  lr=1.88e-04  gpu=7.7GB
step= 1250  loss=0.8523  lr=1.86e-04  gpu=7.7GB
...
step= 1650  loss=0.8783  lr=1.73e-04  gpu=7.7GB

However, we had a brief moment of confusion trying to figure out if this was train loss or validation loss, asking the Artificial Intelligence (AI), "Does our code not record eval loss?" We realized the evaluation loss logging might have been missed, but since the training was already fully complete ("All fine-tuning is complete, proceeding with evaluation"), we immediately moved on to the inference and evaluation (Eval) phase using the latest generated checkpoint models.

Building a Parallel Inference Environment​

We started generation testing using the 20_eval_ft_models.ipynb notebook to see how each model responded to user dialogues. We unified the max_new_tokens for inference to a generous 1024, constantly worrying if another OOM would occur.

But the inference speed was much slower than expected.

"We used two graphics cards for training, so why is inference only using one?"

To utilize 100% of the server's GPU resources, with the AI's help, we wrote a new run_eval_parallel.sh script to process inferences in parallel. This drastically reduced the model inference time, and we successfully built a pipeline that automatically aggregates the inference results and perplexity of each model into an Excel file.

Although an error occurred because VRAM was not properly released when transitioning from DSR1-70B inference to the next model, we resolved it by isolating the environments with the parallel script. Now, it's finally time to compare the actual answer quality of each model!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #13] Limits of 70B Training and the Pivot to Mid-Size Models (HCX, Qwen)
item.content:encoded:
After experiencing the OOM (Out of Memory) hell during the fine-tuning of massive 70B models, on May 4th, we attempted a bold change in strategy. By drastically reducing the batch size, we barely managed to push the 70B models (Llama3.3, DeepSeek-R1) to checkpoint-1200 and 1300, but the training time was absurdly long, resulting in terrible efficiency.

Pivoting to Mid-Size Models (1.5B ~ 9B)​

Considering our physical server resources and the capstone project deadline, we decided it was too risky to rely solely on the 70B models. Therefore, we shifted our focus to relatively lighter mid-size models like HCX-Omni-8B, Qwen35-9B, and HCX-Text-1.5B.

"It's taking a long time to train HCX-Omni-8B, Qwen35-9B, and HCX-Text-1p5B with the current hyperparameters. Are these parameters generally used for these models?" "How does increasing the batch size affect the training?"

Things weren't perfectly smooth just because the models were smaller. To speed up training, we increased the batch size and endlessly debated with the AI to find the optimal hyperparameters for each model size. We first evaluated the training results of the smallest model, HCX-Text-1.5B, to set our tuning direction.

Checkpoint Saving Errors and Kernel Version Issues​

While smoothly training HCX-Omni-8B, we hit another snag while trying to save a checkpoint at step 50.

[RANK 0] Detected kernel version 5.4.0, which is below the recommended minimum of 5.5.0; this can cause the process to hang.
...
![사진 02](./images/02_error.png)

JSONDecodeError Traceback (most recent call last)
---> 60 trainer.train(resume_from_checkpoint=...)

Along with a warning that the OS kernel version was too low and could cause the process to hang, we faced a horrific JSONDecodeError because the saved checkpoint file was corrupted, preventing us from resuming training.

"If the models stop during training, do they resume from where they stopped?"

Fortunately, the Hugging Face Trainer provides a feature to resume training from checkpoints (resume_from_checkpoint), but it's useless if the checkpoint file itself is corrupted. Despite reducing the model size, we spent the entire day wrestling with numerous framework and infrastructure errors. Will we ever reach a stable training orbit?

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #12] 70B Massive Model Fine-Tuning and GPU Memory (OOM) Struggle
item.content:encoded:
On May 3, having gained enough experience with the 8B models, our team finally challenged the ultimate kings of performance: fine-tuning massive 70B (70 billion parameters) models. We attempted to train both Llama 3.3 70B and DeepSeek-R1 70B, but as expected, we hit a massive hardware resource wall.

70B Models and the Terror of OOM (Out of Memory)​

  • Problem: As soon as we ambitiously uploaded and ran the 70B fine-tuning code on the server, errors started popping up.
  • Process:

    "I copied the server's fine_tuning folder and sub-files. Please check the copied files and identify the cause of the error." "Do we not need to modify DeepSeek's 70B model? Please check for potential errors."

  • Result: Our brief moment of relaxation, analyzing train_log.jsonl and asking for estimated completion times, was shattered when the 70B models instantly devoured all the GPU memory. (OOM error occurred!)

The GPU Memory Diet Operation​

  • Problem: "The GPU memory usage is already at MAX." We had to somehow reduce the memory usage so the training wouldn't crash.
  • Process:

    "Modified to save_steps = 50, save_total_limit = 10, eval_steps = 50, patience = 10." "Please evaluate the configured early stopping conditions." "I set the max_seq_length of both 70B models to 512 in ft_configs.yaml, but the server's nvitop still shows memory usage at max. Why is that?"

  • Result: We drastically reduced the context length processed at once (max_seq_length) to 512 and heavily modified hyperparameters to reduce unnecessary saving. However, monitoring with nvitop showed that VRAM was still gasping at its absolute limit. Eventually, the horrific phenomenon of the training freezing around steps 100 and 150 repeated itself.

Taming a massive beast like 70B is truly not easy. We are constantly throwing error logs at the Artificial Intelligence (AI) to find solutions, but it seems we need endless testing to see if we can overcome the physical VRAM limits with software optimization techniques (LoRA, Quantization, etc.). Will we succeed in fine-tuning the 70B models? To be continued in the next log!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #11] Evaluating M6 Model Trained on Synthetic Data (v5)
item.content:encoded:
April 19 is the day we evaluated the performance of the model (M6) trained on the virtual synthetic dataset (v5) we painstakingly created, and wrote the 7th-week weekly report based on it. Was the data we generated while enduring a $10 bill bomb worth it?

A Real Showdown of Model Performance: M0 vs M5 vs M6​

  • Problem: To persuade the advising professor and team members, we needed a weekly report that included quantitative test results and intuitive comparison examples, rather than simply claiming "it got better."
  • Process:

    "Please rewrite the report. The main point is the comparison between M5 based on v4 and M6 based on v5... Include examples of each dataset." "When describing the test results, include explanations with examples of the differences between the un-tuned base model (M0) and M6."

  • Result: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) analyzed the text results generated by the M0, M5, and M6 models and extracted a comparison file (m0_m6_compare.json). The results showed that the base Llama 3.1 model (M0) was somewhat awkward in Korean counseling, and while M5 (trained on refined data v4) improved, it lacked depth. In contrast, the M6 model trained on high-quality synthetic data (v5) perfectly commanded the warm and professional tone typical of a psychological counselor, deeply empathizing with the user's emotions.

The 7th-Week Weekly Report Written by AI (DOCX)​

  • Process:

    "Please write the 7th-week report focusing on the results and significance in two versions (a concise version under 5 pages, and a detailed version). Then generate docx files for each based on the two md files."

  • Result: With a single instruction, two versions (7th-week_report_v1_concise.md, 7th-week_report_v2_detailed.md) were completed in a flash, and even neatly converted into Word files.

Introducing RAG Architecture: FAISS Database (DB) Construction Evaluation​

  • Process:

    "I performed FAISS_DB construction and wrote FAISS_DB_construction_report.docx. Please evaluate our plan and the results of the report."

  • Result: In addition to fine-tuning, which tweaks the model's weights, we introduced a FAISS vector database for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) to reduce hallucinations by referencing external knowledge. I asked the AI to evaluate the structure I built, and received positive feedback (FAISS_DB_evaluation.md).

Today was a day when all the hard work paid off. The thrill of confirming that the trained AI model actually became noticeably smarter is incredible! With model performance proven and the FAISS DB successfully integrated, the Maeumjigi chatbot is one step closer to completion.

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #10] Lifting Application Programming Interface (API) Limits and Resuming Data Synthesis
item.content:encoded:
April 14 is the day we resumed the synthetic data (v5) generation work, which had been temporarily halted since the bill bomb incident. We increased the API billing limit (lifted the restriction) and ran the system, but once again, it didn't go smoothly.

Repairing the Broken Pipeline and Unmanned Automation​

Today was a tough journey of balancing money (API fees), time, and automation scripts for data preprocessing. If the data generation is completed safely, we can finally move on to the next step, right? See you in the next dev log!

item.title: [Maeumjigi Capstone Dev Log #9] Llama 3.1 Fine-Tuning Error Struggle and Week 6 Mid-term Presentation
item.content:encoded:
On April 9, using the Colab notebook we ambitiously completed yesterday, we finally attempted the first training (fine-tuning) of our artificial intelligence model (Llama 3.1). However, reality was not that easy, and we had to face numerous errors. It was also a tough day as we had to simultaneously create the presentation materials for the 6th week of the Capstone Design project.

The Endless Struggle with Colab Fine-Tuning Errors​

  • Problem: As soon as we executed llama31_finetuning_colab.ipynb created yesterday, various errors poured out.
  • Process:

    "Why is an error occurring during M1 fine-tuning in llama31_finetuning_colab (3).ipynb?" "The executed result contains the eos_token. Why is this problem occurring?"

  • Result: A series of problems occurred, such as the special token (eos_token) not being processed correctly when the Artificial Intelligence (AI) model spit out the training data, and memory overflow issues. We repeated the process of copying and pasting the entire error log to Claude to get solutions and modifying the code multiple times. Finally, after many twists and turns, the training was completed, and we were able to extract a meaningful result graph called 학습데이터별학습결과.png!

The AI Assistant's Presentation (PPT) Creation​

  • Problem: While staying up all night training the model, we had to immediately create a PPT on the 6th-week frontend and database progress for the presentation next week.
  • Process:

    "Capstone_Week6_Frontend.pptx is a collection of images introducing the overview so far. Please use this to create a presentation for this week's progress." "Please express the tables of the database design so that the relationships can be seen, referring to the tables implemented in the backend... The table is too large and messy. Please place the User table in the center."

  • Result: Surprisingly, the AI wove the frontend image screenshots together to create a presentation script and slide skeleton. Even when I persistently gave feedback (centering the User table) asking it to draw a complex database ERD (Entity Relationship Diagram) based on the backend code, it perfectly organized and explained the database relationship diagram.

Today was a day to feel the thrill of directly tuning the latest language model called Llama 3.1 with my own hands (and the AI's brain). At the same time, we are learning how to fully utilize AI not only for coding but also for creating presentation materials and designing Database (DB) architecture diagrams.
